other.about: Ship designer (V3 gap item 14, stage 2): the rules that size a ship's parts from what they must do, and the styles that arrange them. A style decides the arrangement and the look, never a size. Numbers marked authored or rough are rules for play and pictures, listed in the fudge register; the drive's own numbers come from the ship record.

crew.why: net habitable volume per person for missions of months; a pressurised module is about twice its net habitable volume once equipment and stowage are in

radiator.why: a flat panel radiates from both faces at emissivity 0.9; area = waste heat / (2 e sigma T^4)

drive_heat.why: combustion heat leaves with the exhaust; the nozzle is cooled by its own propellant
a nuclear thermal reactor is cooled by the propellant it heats while it burns
rough: neutrons from side reactions and bremsstrahlung heat the structure and must be radiated; about a tenth of the jet power
rough: gamma rays caught by the engine's shielding heat it; about a tenth of the jet power

abilities.about: Stage 4: what a ship must do sizes the parts that let it. The kernel's ship_at_world judges each pass; the designer scales a part by the law its figure follows until the figure sits at `margin` of its limit, then asks again.
abilities.margin_why: the same mark the kernel uses for its own 'would pass' advice

shields.name: tiled
shields.why: silica tiles and carbon-carbon leading edges, as on the Space Shuttle; rough limit from radiative equilibrium near 1,600 K

shields.name: PICA
shields.why: phenolic-impregnated carbon ablator; Stardust came back at about 1.2 kW/cm²

shields.name: carbon phenolic
shields.why: the dense ablator of the Galileo probe, which entered Jupiter at about 30 kW/cm²

abilities.nose_over_base_why: Apollo's command module: a 4.7 m spherical nose radius on a 1.96 m base radius
abilities.shield_base_max_why: authored: wider than three hull radii a shield would have to be inflatable or deploy, which the designer does not draw

cd.why: rough hypersonic and subsonic drag coefficients: a blunt capsule face about 1.3 to 1.5, an open truss with modules about 1.2, a pointed skin about 0.5

wing.why: a delta like the Space Shuttle's: aspect about 2.3, landing lift coefficient about 1, lift over drag about 1 on entry; wings longer than one and a half hulls are not drawn (authored)

lifting_body.why: a hull shaped to lift on its own, like the X-24 and HL-10 test craft: less lift per area than a wing

legs.why: the Apollo lunar module's legs took about 3 m/s straight down (10 ft/s)

chute.why: a disk-gap-band supersonic parachute as on Mars landers: drag coefficient about 0.6, opened below Mach 2.2 and 850 Pa; a canopy more than 30 times the ship's frontal area is not carried (authored; Curiosity's was about 23 times)

scoop.why: authored: an intake that fills the tanks in a day of skimming passes through a giant's thin upper air at orbital speed; area = propellant / (density x speed x time)

abilities.shield_emissivity_why: a charred ablator or a tiled face radiates at about 0.85; the pass view shows the face at radiative balance with the peak heating

spine.name: Spine and modules
spine.about: Hard-science: modules strung along an open truss, tanks clustered round it, crew as far from the drive as the spine allows, radiators as flat wings off the middle. Radiator wings are as long as they must be: their area comes from the waste heat, their shape (span over chord) from the style.

skin.why: white thermal blankets on the modules, foil-wrapped tanks, a bare metal truss, black high-emissivity radiators

sleek.name: Sleek hull
sleek.about: High tech: one smooth skin round everything, a long pointed nose, radiators swept back as fins.

skin.why: one gunmetal skin, black radiator fins
